utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around this courtroom. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case IT-09-92-T, the Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness be escorted in the courtroom. Meanwhile, I can briefly deal with P4337, which was 65 ter number 08972, and which was admitted into evidence through Witness Predrag Radic on the 13th of February last year. During the testimony of Nikola Erceg an error was discovered, and the Chamber asked the translation to be reviewed. The revised translation has now been uploaded into e-court under doc ID 03038074-ET. And assuming that the Defence has no objection, but there's always a possibility to revisit the matter within 24 hours, the Court Officer is hereby instructed to replaced existing translation with the revised version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Erceg.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Erceg, before we continue I'd like to remind you that you're still bound by the solemn declaration that you'll speak the truth the whole truth and nothing but the truth. Mr. Traldi will now continue his cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA ERCEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sir, you were asked in the Karadzic case if you were aware of the VRS's devastation of Muslim villages in the ARK, and you testified that you'd seen that in Kozarac in Prijedor municipality every house was destroyed. Do you stand by that evidence today?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA ERCEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, not every house, but many houses were. I had an opportunity there to see a bit more and I had no chance to see other villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Well, can we have 65 ter 32349, page 25.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: As Madam Registrar reminds me, under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: It's labelled under seal because portions of the Karadzic transcript that day are confidential. This page, at least according to my notes, is not one of them. But I'm happy to have it not be broadcast for the moment in an abundance of caution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's have that abundance of caution. It can always be changed later, but I don't know what to expect. Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: As it reflects that it was in open session, I'll simply read out the relevant portion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then if we limit ourselves to this page, then there's no problem. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sir, you're asked at line 6: "Were you aware of the devastation of Muslim villages by the VRS and Bosnian Serb forces?" Now, you first answered no. Then you were asked not at all, and you answered: "Why I would have to know that? I had heard anything about it, could I have believed the story or not. From my personal experience, I saw only Kozarac, every house destroyed. And after a while, as the war went on, one couldn't come even near the front line, so you couldn't know what was going on. And by nature, I'm a pacifist and I didn't want to see these things. If I had the opportunity, I would have avoided it. When I travelled to Prijedor, I saw that village - what's the name? The one I mentioned now? - Kozarac. But I know from stories that things were devastated, one, another, then another. I know it only from stories. I didn't see it." Now first, do you stand behind the truthfulness and accuracy of the portion of your Karadzic testimony that I've just read out to you?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA ERCEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And what it means that you didn't want to see these things, if you had the opportunity you would have avoided, you were intentionally avoiding seeing the kind of destruction that had been wreaked on other villages; right?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA ERCEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I did not have any opportunity to come close to those villages because when I travelled that's not where I was going. I mainly moved from Banja Luka to Belgrade when there was an opportunity for that and from Banja Luka to Pale and back. Once I went to Glamoc where I am from. I never noticed anything there. But that was earlier, so I simply had no opportunity to see that. And that it did happen, that it did occur, I know that it did.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Can we have 65 ter 02382, page 20 in the English and 18 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can the give the number again for the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Actually, for efficiency, can we go to 25 in the English, 23 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: This is a record of the 34th Session of the RS Assembly, and what we're looking at here is the end of the remarks by Mr. Vjestica. And he's expressing concern that -- about a proposal that: "Since it is written in this agreement that everyone will be able to go back to their own territory, that means that his people will be going back to Veliki Babic and we will have to compensate everything we destroyed and burned and 17 mosques that we flattened." Now first, this is an example of the type of destruction that occurred in Kozarac also occurring elsewhere in the ARK; in this case, in Krupa; right?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA ERCEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had no chance to see what happened in the Krupa municipality, but I believe that it was so if this man stated so.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And below that we see President Karadzic begin to speak. Turning to page 26 in the English, 24 in the B/C/S, after he has begun by saying that he was always charmed by Mr. Vjestica, he says just a couple of lines up from the end of the long paragraph: "This is what was said about the control of borders. We will have barbed wire for ten years. We know that." Now, that's a reflection of the intent that the people who had moved out of these areas in response to Mr. Vjestica's concern wouldn't be able, in fact, to come back; right?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA ERCEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Your Honours, I see I'm right around the ten minutes that I'd projected. This I think should be able to be added to P2508, which is excerpts from this session. We'll handle that, for efficiency, later, and I'll have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Traldi. Mr. Lukic, if you're ready for re-examination, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just half a minute, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, the furniture first should be put in place.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Erceg.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA ERCEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I hope that we'll finish everything by 11.30 so that you may then leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can we see P4337, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Erceg, you have seen this decision on the formation of the Crisis Staff of the Autonomous Region of Krajina?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA ERCEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us about this list whether there is anyone in it who is from a different Krajina municipality rather than from Banja Luka or are all these people from Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA ERCEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sajic, Kupresanin, they're all from Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA ERCEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Possibly Kupresanin, he's from Circa, but that's 15 kilometres from Banja Luka. He's from a village that's between Banja Luka and Srbac but mostly it's Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But the duties he discharged were in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA ERCEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was the president of the assembly in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: On transcript page 34000, lines 14 to 16 - that's yesterday's transcript - you said that at the meetings of the Crisis Staff people from various municipalities were often in attendance.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA ERCEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Mostly presidents of Executive Councils and presidents of municipalities and members of parties or of Crisis Staffs of those municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did they actively participate in the work of the Crisis Staff in the sense that they could vote?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA ERCEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: They mostly made proposals. They informed us about the problems in their municipalities and they participated in discussion but they did not vote.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can we now have 1D2837, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It has to do with paragraph 85 of your statement. This document was shown to you in connection with that paragraph. You said that it was a completely autonomous decision of the Crisis Staff of the Sanski Most municipality in paragraph 85. The Prosecutor showed you some documents relating to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We need page 2 of this document, or perhaps even page 3. Yes, it's page 3 in B/C/S and page 2 in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In the introductory part at the top of the page, let's see what the formulations in the document are. The Crisis Staff of the Serbian municipality Sanski Most at its meeting held on 18 May 1992 pursuant to its conclusion under item 1, issued on 20 May 1992 the following order. From the formulations of this document, can we conclude whether it was issued on the basis of some other document or order of the Crisis Staff or was it an autonomous document of the Crisis Staff of the Serbian municipality of Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA ERCEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a document which was issued pursuant to the autonomous decision of the same organ, so it does not rely on any outside document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we continue, if we make such an important matter of "autonomous," then I would have invite both parties to tell me exactly what they understand by "autonomous," because otherwise we lose ourselves in a semantic battle which finally may not assist the Chamber. Mr. Lukic, I am not addressing you or you especially, but I'm also addressing Mr. Traldi in this respect. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. [Interpretation] So -- I have finished with this document. If Mr. Traldi wants to deal with it more, he will have some additional time in the end. Let us now please have a look at P7283. [In English] I would kindly ask to provide Mr. Erceg with his statement from yesterday so he could --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the usher assist, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Erceg, I will ask you something relating to paragraph 80 of your statement. My learned friend Traldi yesterday asked you something connected to the same paragraph and also to the document that we see on our screens right now. So we can see this document from the Banja Luka Crisis Staff. The date is 10 June 1992. "Conclusions," and under item 4, we see that it reads: "Only children, women and the elderly may move out voluntarily, that is to say, of their own free will, from the Autonomous Region of Krajina." My learned friend suggested to you that only Muslims and Croats were implied here, and I will ask you the following:

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I'd object to that characterisation I didn't suggest it applied only to Muslims and Croats though I did suggest that it applied to Muslims and Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let us see. At yesterday's transcript at page 34012, I will read the question of Mr. Traldi. At line 5, it says: "This conclusion restricts the Muslims and Croats who are allowed to go to women, children, and elderly people ..." So we find that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There is a suggestion in it, and not more, not less than that, because it's emphasised that it applies to Muslims and Croats and it doesn't say that applies to others; although, the language Mr. Traldi used does not exclude that. But it could easily be understood as the text being focusing, especially with this questions, as focusing especially on Muslims and Croats. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Erceg, do you see in this document that a distinction is made anywhere between Serbs and non-Serbs?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA ERCEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see such a distinction anywhere, and I'll tell you the historical truth. In the Second World War when it finished, 700.000 people from Krajina moved to Vojvodina. There were strong family ties. I don't know exactly, but I think that between 20 and 30 per cent of the threatened Serbian population moved out to Vojvodina in Serbia. So it's not true that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, I stop you there. You'd like to leave in time. Mr. Lukic asked you whether can you see something in the text. Now, would you please focus your answer on that. Mr. Lukic, I take it that it is a matter of seeing what the text says, and I even wonder whether the parties could not agree on that, that the text itself doesn't make the distinction.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We can agree on this immediately, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I also agree that the text is a blanket proposition.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In this text, under item 4, children, women, and the elderly are enumerated. Only men liable for military service are not included. That's how we see this item 4. That's why I would ask you whether Serbian men could move out of the region of the ARK.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA ERCEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a bit difficult, but, yes, those who were military conscripts could not; others could.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is why I said those who were fit for military service. Who would Serbian men who wanted to leave the territory of the Krajina report to? Did they need to receive any permission; and from whom, if you know?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA ERCEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, a permission was needed for a while. I'm not sure if it was needed throughout the war, but for a while it was necessary, and I'm not sure exactly what sort of a permission it was and whether it -- you needed to get it from military or civilian authorities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: From what you know, though you told us that you didn't know too much about military issues, was it possible to move freely across the confrontation line?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA ERCEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, I have one additional question. You said that for Serbs needed, at least for a certain period of time, they needed permission to leave as well. Now, were the -- was the type of permission given to Serbs, Croats, and Muslims, exactly the same, and were the criteria applied in order to obtain such a permission the same for all three groups as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am not aware of the exact way that the permissions were formulated, so I couldn't tell you that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: On page 34013 of yesterday's transcript - and you don't have to search for that; it's just for the record - you were asked by my learned friend Mr. Traldi in lines 5 and 6, you were aware of the existence of camps in ARK. You said, in line 7: "Yes, military camps ..." You said that you once visited Trnopolje and once you visited Omarska. You went to Trnopolje with Lord, an Englishman, as you said.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA ERCEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know who gave you the permission to visit Trnopolje? Who did you receive that permission from?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA ERCEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: No permission was needed at the time. I think that travel between Banja Luka and Prijedor was normal. We went in Lord's car. I'm not sure what organisation it was. I just heard it was a Lord. We went with them. And as for a permission, I don't think that a permission was needed at the time. Perhaps the reason was that an international organisation had organised the trip.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us please look shortly at P3758. This is the book of minutes from the session of the Kljuc Municipal Assembly Crisis Staff. This document was shown to you yesterday, so let's look at page 2. The Crisis Staff meeting held on the 27th of May, 1992. And it reads: "The Crisis Staff adopted the following conclusions: "1. Legitimacy was given to all decisions of the Crisis Staff of the autonomous region." If the Kljuc Crisis Staff did not give legitimacy to the decisions of the ARK Crisis Staff, what could the ARK Crisis Staff do? Could it replace anyone? Could it punish someone from the Kljuc Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA ERCEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it couldn't because they were completely autonomous with regard to the Crisis Staff of the ARK; if they wanted it to be so, and they were free to act autonomously.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What is true for the parties, of course, is also true for the witness. You are using the word "autonomous," which has various meanings, and it may create some confusion. I leave it to the parties whether they want to seek further clarification or whether we leave it as it is.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps "of their own initiative" instead of "autonomous."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's your testimony. I can't tell you which of the meanings you want to use. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In paragraph 94 of your statement, you say: "Of course, there were situations when municipalities did not see my decisions through, in which case nothing happened. If a municipality asked of us to provide something and we did not have that, nothing happened. If we asked a municipality to do something, which they could not, again, nothing ensued."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, the text you read was not identical with the English translation I have in front of me. You said there were situations when municipalities "did not see my decisions through." Instead of that, I read: "did not carry out my decisions."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: The interpreters' booth does not have the original statement. We were interpreting Mr. Lukic's words.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, I was reading from B/C/S version that was signed --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You should call up the statement of the witness to avoid these problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's have D982 on our screens, please. Let's try with page 25. We need paragraph 90.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We need 94.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So the next page, please, in B/C/S. Thank you. And probably page 15 in English. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do you need 90 or do you need 94.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: 94. I'm sorry. I -- yeah, I corrected it, 94. So let's go --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Page 17 in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In English 17 and next page in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I will read again in B/C/S: "[Interpretation] Of course, there were instances when municipalities did not carry out my decisions, in which case nothing would happen. If a municipality asked us for something that we did not have, nothing would happen. And if we asked a municipality for something that they could not provide, again nothing happened."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I think it corresponds, the translation corresponds now. Thank you. I apologise to the booths. I did not provide them with the statements. I thought that they receive it automatically from our Case Manager.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Concerning this paragraph of your statement, I wanted to show you another document, P6949.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, while we're waiting for that, I'm wondering what you want to do with -- I think it was 1D2837. Do we have that ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It was not tendered, I take it. That was with the -- where you asked from the formulations of this document that you could conclude whether it was issued on the basis of some other document or order. And since you referred to it in rather vague terms, I wonder whether it would not be better for the evaluation of the evidence to have it in evidence or [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We are just checking. If it's not tendered, I would tender it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think what I see is that you then went on wanting to have a look at P7283. But 1D2837 I think was not tendered. If you intend -- Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: This is the one I think that we'd suggested was a duplicate of P2413, and Mr. Lukic didn't tender as a result with a lot with the associated exhibits. Of course, I'd stand to be corrected if I'm misremembering.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we then have that document on our screens so that we can verify whether it's a duplicate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Traldi, could you please repeat the number. It's not properly recorded.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sorry. P2413.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we have that on our screen for a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And one more time so the transcript is correct: 2413.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It's on our list of associated exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is this the one, Mr. Lukic, you're ... referring to a while ago. You only paid attention to whether it was issued on the basis of another document or whether it was not ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you please try to verify that. We'll -- meanwhile, we'll move on and you have an opportunity during the break to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We'll do it during the break, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll wait. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So can we have P6949, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We see here that on the 22nd May, 1992, it was ordered in keeping with the decision of the ARK Assembly in the -- in all municipalities of the ARK, standing operational duty -- or permanent operational duty is being introduced.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA ERCEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It was sent to all companies and social organisations.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA ERCEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What does it actually mean?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA ERCEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: It means to municipal bodies and workers' organisations as well as other institutions that were in existence in the municipalities, such as schools, courts, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What kind of mechanism did you have at your disposal to implement it by force or to sanction unless it is implemented by the municipal organs in Kljuc, Prijedor, or in the companies themselves in the ARK municipalities?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA ERCEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had no authority. It was purely voluntary with the presumption that they will abide by what was prescribed, if necessary. If there was no need, they decided on their own to terminate a particular activity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could ...

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let's briefly look at another document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we do so, could the witness explain by what he meant by "it was purely voluntary." What was voluntary?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If a municipality was in danger for whatever reason, this decision was supposed to be implemented. If there was no threat, then this decision was no longer implemented or the measures were stopped. It primarily dealt with bordering municipalities close to the front lines.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Where does it say so in this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was understood.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You say it -- it's not expressed in document but that's how you understood it. And then you said: "If there was no need, they decided on their own ..." Who's "they" in this context?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If this was the ARK Crisis Staff, it implied the Crisis Staff of the municipality as the body who would decide on, for example, introducing a curfew or not, or some other kind of duty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I'm trying to find where the -- where the duties are described in this document exactly. The first duty I see is that the Crisis Staff is to provide continuous monitoring of the situation giving additional instructions, decisions, and orders. I have some difficulty understanding what you meant when you say, well, you could -- you could not implement it any further. Does that mean that you stopped monitoring?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Times were such that situation changed from one day to the next. We never knew what the next day would be like, so this was extremely flexible and this was the way we felt things should be done. If there was any potential threat, action was to be undertaken either through operational duty or the introduction of curfew or some other measures that would remain in place in a particular municipality for as long as they were necessary. So all documents pertaining to that topic could not be put in a time-frame. They were simply drafted so that we could appropriately address the situation as it arose in a particular municipality. Twenty years down the road, I can't recall any specific details about it, but this would be my general statement when I considered the situation at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I don't find any of that in the text of the document itself. We can move on. But if you have any comment on it, then you are free to give it. Please proceed, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. And we don't have to wait for the break. We just actually -- my colleague checked that 1D2837, 65 ter number, is duplicate of P2413.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for that information. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we have P7285, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: P2 -- sorry. P7285.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Erceg, before us is a document we saw yesterday. My learned friend Mr. Traldi, at transcript page 34020, asked you the following, in line 18. I will read out his question in English and your answer. I quote: [In English] "Now this was done pursuant to a decision of the ARK; right? "A. I'm not sure about that. I don't know if there was an ARK decision." [Interpretation] Looking at the document, do you find any mention of any decision arriving from the Autonomous Region of Krajina.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA ERCEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I'd object on the grounds that this misstates the witness's evidence about the document, and what I have in mind specifically is transcript page 34021, lines 12 through 14.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I think I read from the transcript too. But I'll let my learned friend to clarify it after I finish. I have the answer given by this witness that there is no trace and it's, I think, visible from the document that it does not mention anything from the ARK as a base for this document. I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There was something Judge Orie mentioned that I would like to follow up. Did you monitor the implementation of curfew in the respective municipalities?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA ERCEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. But at the next meeting of the Crisis Staff or some other kind of meeting, we were discussing the situation to see whether anything needed to be done and whether there was any need for assistance. So we discussed these things at meetings, but there was no need for us to be officially notified of the beginning or end of a particular activity.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If you believed that a certain Krajina municipality had to introduce a curfew and they refused, could you remove someone from their position or discipline?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA ERCEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, neither of those. We believed that they were in a position to judge what was best for them and that that was the right solution at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You were asked about a particular document - that is actually P7286 - with regards to Kalinovik and a decision concerning the implementation of a republican-level decision in that municipality. Were you ever in a situation to see any such republican-level decisions being implemented at Kalinovik?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA ERCEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did the municipality of Kalinovik report to you about their work?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA ERCEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If we can see P7288, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Traldi showed you this document where we see that a dispatch arrived from Sarajevo to the CSB in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It's on the second page of this document, so we need ...

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me ask you this: You, personally, in the time-period you referred to before the creation of the corridor, as the president of the Executive Council and a member of the Crisis Staff, what was your communication like with Sarajevo and Pale, if you remember?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA ERCEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was basically no communication. We could communicate only if somebody from Pale, from the bodies there, came to Belgrade when I happened to be there because I had to go there frequently. Then we would meet and discuss particular topics. Other than that, there was no other official possibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: On transcript page 34032, Mr. Traldi mentioned or asked whether the Serbian municipalities were envisaged by the constitution of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina at the time. Did ARK ever hold the prefix Srpska; Serbian?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA ERCEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I'm not sure how it was defined under the constitution, but I don't think it included any need for constitutional arrangements in terms of regional distribution. It was understood that it was to be a Serbian Krajina, but it did not have that attribute in its name.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very well. We won't go any deeper into any constitutional discussions. Yesterday, Mr. Traldi read out a part of your interview provided to the OTP. It was transcript page 34039. He focused, in particular, on Mr. Brdjanin having good co-operation with the republican level. You were then asked who with exactly, and you said: Well, it was a personal matter. He co-operated well with the SDS president and deputies in the assembly. They were on good terms. You were unable to say how important it was, but you did say that there was a common goal they all shared. Then Mr. Traldi asked you whether you stand by that, and you confirmed as much. Let me ask you this now: In your view, what is the common goal that united those people?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA ERCEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had in mind the most important or the single goal, which was that it should remain as part of Yugoslavia as it existed after Croatia and Slovenia left. So that Republika Srpska would remain a part of Yugoslavia. At that time, when we had discussions with Alija Izetbegovic, we were actually discussing the possibility of his being appointed the first president of that new entity. We tried our utmost to remain within the framework of Yugoslavia by using political means, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'd like to show you P431. This document is the original minutes of the Assembly of the Serbian People in BH. The date is --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could Mr. Lukic repeat the date, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Held on 12 May, 1992. At transcript page 34046, part of English page 20 was read out. It is on page 16 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And 20 in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What was read out were the words of Mr. Vjestica, where he says -- I will read it out: "On the right-hand side of the Una river there are no more Muslims left in the municipality of Bosanska Krupa. All of the municipalities there were" --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Mr. Lukic will need to indicate that place on the page. We are unable to find it at this speed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, I don't know how long it will be, but we are close to the time for a break.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Maybe it will help. Maybe I could find exactly where on this page is. Now I am a bit lost.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then perhaps organise yourself and then let's deal with it after the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, we'll take a break of 20 minutes, and we'd like to see you back after that. You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: However before the break I would like to briefly address a matter of procedural hygiene, I would say, and that is the objection made by -- the objection made by Mr. Traldi. Mr. Traldi objected to a question in which, as he said, Mr. Lukic did not accurately quote the evidence of the witness, misstated the evidence of the witness. Now, the subject matter was the following: Whether decisions taken on a lower level find their origin in a previous decision taken by a higher level organ. There are a few options. Either the decision itself refers to such a decision, then it's visible from the document; or you draw conclusions on the basis of chronology, subject matter, and often similarity in text. Now, that was the issue which apparently led to the objection. What then happened is the following. Mr. Traldi said more or less that you have ignored another part, which I had on my mind. Mr. Lukic, you responded to that, and you said I think I read from the transcript too. You're perfectly right. That's what you did. Although, it's not an answer to a possible misstating, because you can distort something in context. But let's leave all that aside. I'm inclined to think that you are right, although not a response. Then, Mr. Lukic, you continued: "But I'll let my learned friend to clarify it after I finish." That's usually a decision I take. And, of course, I highly appreciate that you're assisting me in performing my task, I would ask you to leave that to me after I have decided on the objection. You then continued by saying: "I have the answer given by this witness that there's no trace" in it. And then you see, I started with an analysis of what the problem was. Mr. Traldi was posing his questions yesterday on the basis first he said did you know, the witness said I didn't know. Then he put a few documents to the witness. And then the witness agreed on basis of chronology, subject matter, that it originated from elsewhere. And then your question, Mr. Lukic, was about whether the document shows, so yes or no, whether it's visible in the document, which - and that's why I started with the analysis - are two different aspects of the same problem. Okay. So you said I have the answer given by this witness that there's no trace in it, I think visible from the document, that it doesn't mention anything from the ARK as a basis for this document. So what did you is not responding to the objection but after you've told Mr. Traldi what he could do later on. Now you repeat the evidence of the witness and you express that you are satisfied by it, which I understand that you are satisfied by it, but it's not really a response to an objection. And then you said I'll move on. Now, that last line, again, is something -- you can move on as soon as I have allowed you to move on. I'm just trying to analyse what it was that happened, and I'm also analysing what happened here in court. That's what I call procedural hygiene. Let's next time respond to an objection, I'll then rule on the objection and I may give some guidance for the other party how to proceed, and then with my permission everyone can proceed. I consider it important to have clear rules on how we act in this courtroom, and I took this just as an example. Finally, we had exactly the same issue earlier today, whether it was visible from a document that originated from a previous decision taken by someone else. Then the parties within a second could agree on it and therefore didn't have to bother the witness with all that, and I wondered whether all that could not have been done in relation to this document as well. I added perhaps five -- I wouldn't say wasted minutes but at least five additional minutes to something that should perhaps not have happened as it happened. We take a break and we resume at five minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: While we are waiting for the witness to be escorted in the courtroom, we have a similar -- also another translation issue. The Prosecution, that's at least the information the Chamber received, the Prosecution has received a revised English translation of P07287, which was MFI'd. That's 65 ter 19104. The document was MFI'd through Witness Erceg on the 1st of April. I'll finish this after we've --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'll just continue. The portion in bold at the beginning of the article was missing in the English and this has now corrected in the revised the translation, as we understand. The revised translation has been uploaded into e-court under doc ID 02029664-ET. And if the Defence has no objection, the Prosecution, as we understand, request that the Court Officer be instructed to replace the existing translation with the revised version and that the document be admitted. This instruction is hereby given and P7287 is admitted into evidence. When I earlier said this morning that P3343 was admitted into evidence, that was superfluous because it had been admitted already. Only the English translation had to be replaced. We'll now continue, Mr. Erceg. Mr. Lukic will now continue his re-examination. Mr. Lukic, may I take it that you'll conclude so much before 11.30 that Mr. Traldi has an opportunity to put some of --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I spoke with my colleague, Mr. Traldi, so ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Booths were correct. We did not have correct page in B/C/S. We should need the next page, 17 in B/C/S. And we are on the correct page in English, only we'll need the bottom page of English version. In B/C/S it's 17th line from the top, and in English version it's line 8 from the bottom. The very end of the line in English, and last third of line in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So it's noted that Mr. Vjestica said: "On the right bank of the Una river there are no Muslims in the Serbian municipality of Bosanska Krupa. All the enclaves that were there, Rapusa, Veliki Vrbovik, Ostroznica, Babic, Muslim Jasenica, and Zavir, we have evacuated them so that there will be none there for the duration of war operations. Will they have a place to return to? I think not [sic] as our president told us the happy news that the right bank of the Una is the border." And I will read on from the transcript from page --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Before do you so, just one clarification.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You read "I think not," in that way it was interpreted to us, but in the English translation we read "I think it is unlikely" after "our president told us."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Sometimes we correct the written translation when we think it's not the best.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So I will read from the transcript my learned friend Traldi's question, page 34046, line 13, and I quote: [In English] "Q. Now, what Mr. Vjestica is saying here is that because of the territorial objective, the fourth objective set out by President Karadzic, the Muslims who have left that area won't be able to come back; right?" "A. Yes, but it is based on a fact that in the materials in possession of the Muslim and Croat side is also written that the Serbs who had left the areas that they control have no right to come back either. "Q. So is it right, then, that you agree that the policy was that Muslims and Croats who left couldn't come back but you assert that Muslims and Croats, their authorities had similar policies about Serbs who had left. Is that your evidence? "A. Yes, yes." It continues and question is, and I quote: "Now, in paragraph 74 of your statement, you say, in pertinent part about people who left that it's clear that everyone had the right to their property even after moving out. Now, you don't really know whether people who left maintained any right to their property, do you? "A. I think that they had documentation which was sufficient at the time stipulating that they can come back and keep their property, especially since it was all recorded in land registers that had not been tampered with during the war." [Interpretation] In paragraph 102 of your statement, you say that the property of those who had left Banja Luka was temporarily assigned to others, that the property was listed so that it could be returned in full to the rightful owner. This was a long introduction and excuse me for that. But I would now ask you the following during the war, during war operations, are you aware of there having been any requests on part of Muslims and Croats to return to the territory that was under the control of the Serbian forces?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA ERCEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were individual cases like that. I heard that at assembly meetings. We would discuss all sorts of issues so I heard about this too. So there were individual instances, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And do you know what was done then?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA ERCEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wouldn't know any details about that, but there were such requests.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Were there requests for large-scale return?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA ERCEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not hear about any such instances at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And was anyone's return prevented after the war, if you know?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA ERCEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can I get clarification. The -- witness now you are saying no. A few minutes ago you said I wouldn't know any details about that. How do you know that they could -- they were not prevented if you didn't know what happened?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This is after the war, Your Honour, I asked.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have understood that the Defence counsel asked me two different questions relating to two different time-periods, as far as I understood. Maybe I have misunderstood.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. My apologies.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And just briefly, because we should wrap it up soon, on transcript page 34050, my learned friend Traldi asked you the following, and I shall quote: [In English] "And you were aware that there were forced expulsions of Muslims and Croats from ARK; right?" "A. Yes. But please, not forced, judging by the records provided by any institution, but one neighbour would expel another for God knows which reasons. I'm just stating that as an example." Can you give us an example from your life from that time of a situation in which you were present when someone tried to expel somebody else or did you have a chance to take part in that and in what way? Just briefly.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA ERCEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were some such instances. A specific example was the occasion when I saved a Croat so that he wouldn't have to leave his flat.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Erceg. This was all that we had for you. Now my learned friend Mr. Traldi will ask you a few questions. I don't know if they informed you, I couldn't do that, I should see you before you leave The Hague, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And in light of the witness's schedule, I'll try to be very, very efficient. I expect I won't need more than five minutes. If we could have first 65 ter 22817a. This a transcript of a video. For efficiency, I'm just going to go to the part of the transcript I'm interested in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, before we look at that. I would seek one clarification of the last answer the witness gave in response to a question. You're recorded as having answered: "Yes, there were some such instances. A specific example was the occasion when I saved a Croat so that he wouldn't have to leave his flat." Who did that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A Croat, Ivan Vortnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And who saved him that he wouldn't have to leave his flat? Oh, he --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He came to me and asked me to see if there was any possibility for him to remain in his flat and I said I'll try. I'll go to the municipal authorities, I'll address the persons who need to be addressed, and he stayed in his apartment. That was just one example. There were hundreds of such examples in each municipality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, it's not an example of people being expelled by they're neighbours. But, Mr. Lukic, you've asked that question. It has been answered. Let move on Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Can we have page 2 in both languages, please. Further cross-examination by Mr. Traldi:

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And, sir, you discussed on re-examination the movement out of the Serb population from the ARK during World War II. Here, we see a transcript of an interview with Mr. Karadzic, and in the last quote before the redaction he refers, among other things, to 5300 Serbs in Sanski Most who were killed during World War II. It says in Bosanska Krupa and Bihac the Serbs had been majority beforehand. And he says Grmec, Kozara, and the Sana river valley have always been exclusively Serbian. It's correct that the Bosnian Serb leadership took the position that areas that had been Serb majority before World War II, including such areas in the ARK, had to be Serb-controlled during and after the war; right?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA ERCEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And Grmec, Kozara, and the Sana river valley, that's a reference particularly to the municipalities of Prijedor and Sanski Most; right?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA ERCEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, I'd tender 65 ter 22817a.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 22817a receives number P7294, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Finally, sir, regarding the issue of voluntary departure that you discussed again on re-examination, you stood today by your testimony in the Karadzic case that every house in Kozarac was destroyed and that you'd heard about the destruction of other villages in the ARK. You confirmed yesterday that people in prisons behind barbed wire were living in terror. So what I'm putting to you is that you cannot possibly have believed then or now that the people whose homes were destroyed and the people living in terror in camps had any choice but to leave if they had the money to pay and they were given permission to go. You know there was nothing voluntary about it. That's the truth; right?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA ERCEG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Traldi. Mr. Erceg, this concludes your evidence in this court. I'd like to thank you very much for coming a long way to The Hague, and of course we are glad that we could accommodate your return today so that you didn't have to stay any further in The Hague. I'd like that thank you for having answered all the questions that were put to you, put you to the parties, put to you by the Bench, and I wish you a safe return home again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may follow the usher. And, Mr. Lukic, may I take it that you want to be excused in view of what you said earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: May I be excused?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, you are excused, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We need hygiene kept well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I didn't say that I requested your to be excused but I assumed and you confirmed that. Thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And, Mr. President, if I might also be excused, though for a different reason.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we had one leftover of yesterday in relation to 65 ter 14584, which was not further addressed in court and which was related to Witness Vidoje Blagojevic. And I think I yesterday asked the Defence whether it withdraws the tendering of the document, and I have not yet received an answer. Mr. Stojanovic, are you able to give that, or would you wait until Mr. Lukic is back?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right, Your Honour. I think that he was in charge of this part that has to do with Mr. Blagojevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Is the next witness available? You would call Mr. Pero Andric as your next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I think that he is ready.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could the witness be escorted in the courtroom. I see the usher is -- has left the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I see a lot of counsel for the Prosecution standing, but it's -- it will be you?

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Yes, good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours. It's Matthew Gillett addressing the next witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Andric. Can you hear me in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can hear you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before you give evidence, the Rules require that you make a solemn declaration of which the text is now handed out to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Andric. Please be seated. Mr. Andric, you'll first be examined by Mr. Stojanovic. You find Mr. Stojanovic to your left. Mr. Stojanovic is counsel for Mr. Mladic. Please proceed, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, I would ask you to speak slowly and tell us your full name.

utterances.speaker: PERO ANDRIC
utterances.text: Pero Andric.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Would you please tell the Court when and where you were born?

utterances.speaker: PERO ANDRIC
utterances.text: 11th February, 1971; Srebrenica municipality; Pribicevac, place of birth.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Andric, please tell the Chamber what education you have.

utterances.speaker: PERO ANDRIC
utterances.text: I'm an electrician by occupation.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Where do you currently work?

utterances.speaker: PERO ANDRIC
utterances.text: I currently work at the lead and zinc mine Sase, Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you have any military education, Mr. Andric?

utterances.speaker: PERO ANDRIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Up until the breakout of the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina, did you serve the compulsory military service?

utterances.speaker: PERO ANDRIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Would you please tell the Chamber where and what your military occupational speciality was.

utterances.speaker: PERO ANDRIC
utterances.text: I served at Skopje, the Petrovac airport, and my military occupational speciality was rocket mechanic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Where were you when the war broke out in 1992? Where were you living at the time?

utterances.speaker: PERO ANDRIC
utterances.text: I lived at the Pribiceva village where I was born.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you at any point join the armed forces of Republika Srpska; that is to say, were you mobilised?

utterances.speaker: PERO ANDRIC
utterances.text: I was mobilised in 1992, but I don't know the exact dates.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell the Chamber to which unit you were mobilised.

utterances.speaker: PERO ANDRIC
utterances.text: I don't know how exactly the units were called. It was a village guard of some sort. One could call it that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: After that, was there any organised military formation that you belonged to in terms of establishment over time?

utterances.speaker: PERO ANDRIC
utterances.text: Yes. After that, I was a member of companies and eventually I was a member of a military police platoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Would you please tell the Chamber which brigade it was that you were -- belonged to.

utterances.speaker: PERO ANDRIC
utterances.text: I think it was the 3rd Battalion of the Bratunac Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you have to perform any duties of an officer in the 3rd Battalion of the Bratunac Brigade?

utterances.speaker: PERO ANDRIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us at least the year, if not anything closer, in terms of the point in time when you left the 3rd Battalion and were transferred to the military police platoon?

utterances.speaker: PERO ANDRIC
utterances.text: I think it was in 1994 that I joined the military police platoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And this military police platoon, which brigade did it belong to?

utterances.speaker: PERO ANDRIC
utterances.text: The Bratunac Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you also tell us until when did you remain in that military police platoon?

utterances.speaker: PERO ANDRIC
utterances.text: I think, as far as I remember, that it was until June, around the 15th or 16th, I don't know the exact dates, but in 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Just for the record, did you say June or July 1995?

utterances.speaker: PERO ANDRIC
utterances.text: May ... May, June, July.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Just take it slowly. That's precisely why I would like you to tell us for the record in which month did you cease to be a member of the military police platoon?

utterances.speaker: PERO ANDRIC
utterances.text: In June.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. After that, did you perform certain tasks? In other words, were what your duties until the end of the war?

utterances.speaker: PERO ANDRIC
utterances.text: You mean after the military police?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, after.

utterances.speaker: PERO ANDRIC
utterances.text: I was engaged in the work of civilian services in Srebrenica on different jobs.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Please tell the Court what kind of work did you perform in Srebrenica town and its environs.

utterances.speaker: PERO ANDRIC
utterances.text: At first, we worked on touring Slapovici which is a small town of weekend homes. Later on, we cut wood. After that, I participated in the work of the commission for war booty.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Was that under the remit of the civilian structures in Srebrenica or the army?

utterances.speaker: PERO ANDRIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I was engaged by the municipal civilian authorities. At least I believed they were civilian.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: By that time, had any members of your immediate family been killed?

utterances.speaker: PERO ANDRIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Who was killed in terms of your immediate family?

utterances.speaker: PERO ANDRIC
utterances.text: My brother.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: When and where?

utterances.speaker: PERO ANDRIC
utterances.text: In 1994 on the 18th of November in Bihac. That is, the Bihac theatre of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Your engagement with the civilian structures of Srebrenica municipality, did it have anything to do with the fact that a member of your immediate family was killed?

utterances.speaker: PERO ANDRIC
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Just to intervene at this stage. I'm looking at the revised 65 ter summary for the witness and not seeing a reference to working with civilian structures or this topic in general, so I'm just wondering if my friend could direct me to any notice of this topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. I think my learned friend is correct. It is not in the submission. I just wanted to go through his biographical details, so this was the last I had to ask of that particular topic. My purpose was simply to finish off the topic of his engagement with the civilian structures during the war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It's still relevant to have that in a 65 ter summary. But if that's what have you done now, we can't -- please then move on and try to find the subject matter which we find in the 65 ter summary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Before you do so, Mr. Stojanovic --

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Precisely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: -- let me just point out to you that that very last question that caused Mr. Gillett to stand up was a leading question.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll bear that in mind, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- so that I do not put leading questions anymore.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I'd like to direct your attention, Mr. Andric, to a specific time-period concerning fighting in Srebrenica. Do you recall when the fighting around Srebrenica started in 1995?

utterances.speaker: PERO ANDRIC
utterances.text: It began in July on the 11th, as far as I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: To the best of your recollection, what was your task on the 11th of July, 1995?

utterances.speaker: PERO ANDRIC
utterances.text: As far as I recall on the 11th of July, a group of military policemen was securing the road between Sase and Pribicevac. A military convoy or some military personnel were supposed to travel along that road, although I don't know who exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: As far as you remember, who was in that group of military policemen executing that task?

utterances.speaker: PERO ANDRIC
utterances.text: I don't recall any specific names. I just know there were five or six of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: What was your task specifically while securing the road?

utterances.speaker: PERO ANDRIC
utterances.text: Well, we had to secure the road, make it safe, so that the military personnel, the officers, could go through. We were told that the personnel would include General Mladic himself. It was a forested area, and we were supposed to secure the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: How long did you stay performing that task that day?

utterances.speaker: PERO ANDRIC
utterances.text: The group of vehicles that passed through did not --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could the witness kindly repeat his answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness repeat his answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We stayed in that place until the establishment group of officers went back. So when they returned, we returned towards the evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you this: Please tell the Court where this column of vehicles with VRS officers went at first. In what direction?

utterances.speaker: PERO ANDRIC
utterances.text: In the direction of Pribicevac, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Were you performing that task all the way up until the column returned from Pribicevac?

utterances.speaker: PERO ANDRIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In what direction did the column travel from Pribicevac?

utterances.speaker: PERO ANDRIC
utterances.text: Towards Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: What was your task the next day, on the 12th of July?

utterances.speaker: PERO ANDRIC
utterances.text: On the 12th of July, I don't know who went exactly, but we were in Potocari where the Muslim population surrendered and where the prisoners were transported. We provided security to General Mladic in the outer parameter. We were not in his immediate detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: To the best of your recollection, please tell the Court what was the time of day on the 12th of July when you arrived Potocari?

utterances.speaker: PERO ANDRIC
utterances.text: I don't know exactly. It was sometime in the afternoon. Midday perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: What do you remember, in terms of events in Potocari?

utterances.speaker: PERO ANDRIC
utterances.text: What I remember is that there were many refugees; women, children, other people. I remember that General Mladic addressed them. He talked to them, telling them that they would be taken to the place they wanted to go. I think he gave some drink and food to some of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you observe any UN or UNPROFOR members close by?

utterances.speaker: PERO ANDRIC
utterances.text: Yes, they were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Were they engaged in any activity while you were in Potocari in terms of escorting -- while you were there escorting General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: PERO ANDRIC
utterances.text: I don't know what they were doing. I just noticed they were present.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: While you were there, was the population supplied with food, water, or any other necessity?

utterances.speaker: PERO ANDRIC
utterances.text: I observed that General Mladic himself gave them something. He threw packs of juice in the crowd, but that was all I could see at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Were there any other VRS officers, commanding personnel, in Potocari at the time?

utterances.speaker: PERO ANDRIC
utterances.text: Yes, but I don't know who they were.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could the witness be asked to approach the microphone. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, could you come a bit closer to the microphone, please. Perhaps if the chair -- the back of the chair would be adjusted, it would be easier for the witness to ... Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. May I continue, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: How long did you stay in Potocari?

utterances.speaker: PERO ANDRIC
utterances.text: I don't know exactly. Perhaps two to three hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: While you were there, did you notice if there were any able-bodied men in the crowd of people gathered there?

utterances.speaker: PERO ANDRIC
utterances.text: I think there were.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you notice that there was any separation of those men from the elderly, children and women?

utterances.speaker: PERO ANDRIC
utterances.text: I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Please tell the Court how long you stayed in Potocari? What was the time of day when you left?

utterances.speaker: PERO ANDRIC
utterances.text: I think we returned to Bratunac sometime in the afternoon. I don't know precisely when. I don't recall such details any longer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: The next day, if you can tell us to the best of your recollection, what was your task?

utterances.speaker: PERO ANDRIC
utterances.text: The next day, I and a group of military policemen went with General Mladic to Srebrenica via Potocari. That is how we reached Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: As a member of the MP platoon, who issued tasks to you specifically?

utterances.speaker: PERO ANDRIC
utterances.text: I don't remember that since I have no particular duty. We probably received it from the commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Who commanded the MP platoon at the time in the Bratunac Brigade?

utterances.speaker: PERO ANDRIC
utterances.text: I think it was Mirko Jankovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know someone named Momir Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: PERO ANDRIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: What was his duty at the time, his position?

utterances.speaker: PERO ANDRIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, he was a security officer in charge of security affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you receive specific orders or tasks from him at any point in time?

utterances.speaker: PERO ANDRIC
utterances.text: I did not, but I can't speak for others.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: When you say you knew Momir Nikolic, can you describe for the Court what was the extent of your acquaintance? How long did you know him?

utterances.speaker: PERO ANDRIC
utterances.text: Only during the time I was in the military police. I didn't know him before that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When following General Mladic while he was on the move, what did you use? How did you move?

utterances.speaker: PERO ANDRIC
utterances.text: We used a military vehicle behind General Mladic's vehicle. Ours was called Pinzgauer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you remember how many members of the MP platoon were included in that task?

utterances.speaker: PERO ANDRIC
utterances.text: I don't know exactly. Perhaps five or six.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember whether on that second day the column, including you and General Mladic, stopped in Potocari?

utterances.speaker: PERO ANDRIC
utterances.text: We did not stop. We just passed through Potocari.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you at any point in time move towards Suceska and Vijogor village?

utterances.speaker: PERO ANDRIC
utterances.text: We did.

utterances.speaker: MR. GILLETT
utterances.text: Your Honours, I was a bit slow to react just because there's not a great space between the question and answer, but we are entering substantive matters and that was a leading question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Would you refrain from leading from now on, Mr. Stojanovic. Even if there's no objection, it may not strengthen the probative value of the testimony of the witness if you continually put leading questions to him. But now there is an objection and specifically related to -- to the stage we're now moving to. So would you please refrain and proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Andric, please tell the Court what you remember in terms of visiting those two locations?

utterances.speaker: PERO ANDRIC
utterances.text: What I remember is that we were in Srebrenica in front of the municipal building, the church, and that we went to that settlement of Suceska or in its direction. I don't know exactly. Close to a gas station, we took on board some women, elderly Muslim women. That's what I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Why did you bring them inside your vehicle?

utterances.speaker: PERO ANDRIC
utterances.text: General Mladic personally ordered us to do so. They were in front of the building sitting down exhausted. They were all elderly, and we were told to take them inside our vehicle and drop them off in Potocari close to the UN compound.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did those elderly exhausted women ask to be taken to Potocari?

utterances.speaker: PERO ANDRIC
utterances.text: I don't remember them asking. They were old women. They didn't ask for anything. We simply took them on board and drove off.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: What were your movements following your visit to the locations you mentioned a moment ago?

utterances.speaker: PERO ANDRIC
utterances.text: I think we returned to Bratunac --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mladic, you shouldn't speak aloud. You know that. So refrain from doing that. I see that there may be a problem that there's no other counsel available. I would say if one, perhaps, of your team, Mr. Stojanovic, could keep a close eye on Mr. Mladic that if he wants to consult, that he can give a hint without speaking aloud because that's not acceptable. Could you please do that. It seems to me that Mr. Mladic, at this moment, wants to consult with you. At the same time, we are so close to the time for a break that we could consider to take that break now so that you have an ample opportunity do that. But whatever consultations will take place, not at an audible volume. Would you like to take the break now?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Certainly, Your Honour. We may take a break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll take a break. We'll take a break of 20 minutes, and we'd like to see you back after the break, Witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We take the break, and we'll resume at ten minutes past midday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Andric, we stopped at one point when you were telling us about your second visit to Srebrenica and when you were in front of the church and then passed through Potocari. Would you please tell me whether someone entered the church in Srebrenica on that occasion, to visit it?

utterances.speaker: PERO ANDRIC
utterances.text: I only went to the door and looked inside. I don't know whether anyone else entered.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you notice anything that was typical on the building itself?

utterances.speaker: PERO ANDRIC
utterances.text: It was devastated; a badly damaged church. I don't know anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Would you please tell me whether there was anything characteristic that you remember about the events in and around the church at that point while you were visiting the church?

utterances.speaker: PERO ANDRIC
utterances.text: I only glanced inside. I heard from others that it was devastated. I did not enter, and I had heard that cattle was kept in the church too.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Were any shots fired or heard at any moment?

utterances.speaker: PERO ANDRIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: After Srebrenica, where did you travel on?

utterances.speaker: PERO ANDRIC
utterances.text: Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: What was your next task on that day?

utterances.speaker: PERO ANDRIC
utterances.text: I don't remember exactly. I think that we were carrying out usual everyday activities, but I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell me where you spent the afternoon after you returned from Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: PERO ANDRIC
utterances.text: I don't know exactly. I can't remember. I know that we were also in front of the church in Bratunac, in front of the brigade command. And after that, unless I'm wrong about the dates, I think that we set out towards Konjevic Polje and Vlasenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us to the best of your recollection what time of day was it when you set out towards Vlasenica?

utterances.speaker: PERO ANDRIC
utterances.text: I think it was in the afternoon, but I wouldn't know the exact time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
